source.title: Alice in Wonderland: Simple Tasks Showing Complete Reasoning Breakdown in State-Of-the-Art Large Language Models
source.authors: Marianna Nezhurina; Lucia Cipolina-Kun; M. Cherti; J. Jitsev

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the supplementary material. Some figures and plots are flattened or garbled in the extracted text, so exact plotted values cannot always be assigned.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream task accuracy across model scales, which bears on V6, but it does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports AIW reasoning-task performance and comparisons across model scales, not pretraining loss, token-count or compute sweeps, or compute-optimal allocations. Cited scaling-law findings are background, not results from this study. AIW Light control results and other task results are not included unless they bear on the scale-to-downstream-performance comparison.
record.test_reason: The study tests models of different sizes, within the same family, on a new set of simple reasoning tasks (AIW). It reports how downstream accuracy changes with scale, which bears on V6. It does not measure loss, fit any curve, or relate accuracy to pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. T3 (new setting) fits better than T2: the study does not aim at the scaling-law question with a different method, it only compares scales on its own tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find an advantage for larger pretraining scale on AIW tasks, but all models show low or strongly fluctuating accuracy on simple structure-preserving variations. They also argue that current standardized benchmarks, possibly contaminated, cannot properly serve as downstream tasks for measuring scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates answer accuracy on AIW reasoning problems across existing models; it does not measure held-out loss or reproduce the original scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: AIW problem variation and problem version substantially change correct-response rates; prompt type also changes average accuracy, though the paper reports fluctuations across variations under multiple prompt types.

fits_no_version.finding: MMLU, GSM8k, MATH, ARC-c and HellaSwag scores do not predict AIW accuracy: many models score high on the benchmarks but near 0 on AIW (Fig. 8, Suppl. Tab. 12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Performance on one downstream benchmark predicts performance on other downstream reasoning tasks.

record.code_released: AIW repo (URL not stated in the text)
record.problems: The study evaluates a limited set of AIW templates and reports that variation diversity and count are insufficient. The scale comparisons are not controlled loss measurements or fitted scaling curves; many model sizes are unknown, and plotted values are not always available as exact text values. The authors also raise possible test-data leakage for some models and versions.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional AIW task results, prompt conditions, controls, and individual model performances. They were left out where they do not directly compare model scale with downstream accuracy, or where the relevant plotted rates are not stated in text and would exceed the useful scale-comparison rows. Scale-related comparisons are summarized in Sections 3.4.2–3.4.3 and Figures 22–24 and 31.

untested.parts: Relation of downstream accuracy to pretraining loss, any fitted or predictive scale-to-accuracy curve, and parameter counts for the closed models.
All of V1: no loss measured.

missing.what: AIW Light control problems show a scale advantage among small Qwen 2.5 and Llama 3.1 models, where AIW itself gives no signal: larger models have higher averages and smaller fluctuations.
Overall ranking on the AIW test set by average rate and robustness score R: Llama 3.1 70B and Qwen 2.5 32B fall in the very low group, while the 405B/72B models reach only the low group.
Smaller models (<13B) stay at or below about p=0.1, roughly random-guess level, while large closed models exceed p=0.3 on AIW original.
Larger o1-preview robustly outperforms smaller o1-mini, despite benchmark claims that the two are comparable.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study. The scale comparisons are qualitative and drawn from plots. Many model sizes are unknown, and scale is confounded with model generation and post-training; Llama 2 70B outranks Llama 3.1 70B on average rate (Fig. 26).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens, and its trend with compute.
Architecture-shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study evaluates AIW-task accuracy across model scales, but does not relate performance to pretraining loss or fit a predictive scale-to-performance curve.
Effects of parameter counting, schedules, data, fitting methods, exponents, or curve bending on fitted scaling laws.

rows.subject: GPT-4o / GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3 Opus / Claude 3 Sonnet comparison
rows.operation_detail: Compared AIW downstream task accuracy for smaller and larger model counterparts.

conditions.value: AIW original, AIW Ext, and AIW Friends
Correct-response rates averaged across problem versions and variations

rows.baseline: GPT-4o-mini and Claude 3 Sonnet: below p = 0.1
rows.value: GPT-4o and Claude 3 Opus: above p = 0.3
rows.note: The text gives these group-level comparisons but no individual rates here. The authors report a larger/smaller scale performance gap on these tasks; exact sizes are not stated.
rows.check: For both pairs, the larger model clearly outperforms the smaller one: averaged over tasks and variations, the larger is above p=0.3 and the smaller below p=0.1 (Fig. 22D). Parameter counts for all four models are unknown; the authors treat them as larger/smaller counterparts. State changed from partial to observed for the direction of the effect.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 family (8B–405B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared AIW downstream task performance across model scales in the family.

conditions.value: AIW original, AIW Ext, and AIW Friends

rows.value: The authors report higher correct-response rates with larger scale, alongside strong fluctuations across problem variations and versions.
rows.note: The prose describes the scale trend and fluctuations; individual plotted values are not recoverable from the extracted figure text.
rows.check: Higher scale gives higher rates, but small models sit near 0 and gains appear only at the largest scales. Fig. 27 places Llama 3.1 70B in the very low group. The authors suspect training-data leakage for Llama 3.1 405B on AIW original. Baseline should be the smaller family members, near 0.

rows.subject: Recent reasoning models, including distilled models at 7B/8B, 32B, and 70B
rows.stage_stated: Reasoning-model training; the compared distilled models use supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream AIW performance across reasoning-model scales and training approaches.

conditions.value: AIW Friends, AIW Plus, and AIW Circles Colleagues
Distilled models at different scales, standard SOTA LLMs, and reasoning models

rows.measure: Average correct-response rate and unified robustness score R
rows.baseline: Standard SOTA LLMs and smaller-scale distilled models: below 0.2
rows.value: Larger-scale distilled models: mid-range 0.4 < p, R < 0.6; the authors state larger-scale distilled models generally perform significantly better than 7B/8B models, with a noted exception for R1-Qwen-32B.
rows.note: This comparison involves different training regimes as well as scale, and the reported pattern is not a fitted or isolated scaling relationship.
rows.check: Scale is confounded with base model (Llama 3.3 70B vs Llama 8B; Qwen 32B vs Qwen 7B), with distillation data and with post-training. The authors note exceptions: R1-Qwen-32B, and R1-Llama-8B vs 70B on Circles Colleagues. The baseline merges standard LLMs with small distilled models.

source_check.correct: Figure 31 places larger distilled reasoning models at 0.4 < p, R < 0.6 with an explicit exception for R1-Qwen-32B. Standard SOTA LLMs and smaller distilled reasoning models are below 0.2. Figure 30 also identifies R1-Llama-8B versus R1-Llama-70B as an exception to the larger-model advantage on AIW Circles Colleagues.
